passages.happening:
News of Jericho and Ai spreads, and the peoples of the land answer it in two ways. The kings west of the Jordan join forces: ‘they came together to wage war against Joshua and Israel’ (verse 2).

The people of Gibeon choose another course. They ‘acted deceptively’ (verse 4). They send envoys loaded with worn-out sacks, cracked and mended wineskins, patched sandals, threadbare clothes, and bread that is dry and moldy.

At the camp at Gilgal they say, “We have come from a distant land; please make a treaty with us” (verse 6). The men of Israel are wary: “Perhaps you dwell near us. How can we make a treaty with you?” (verse 7).

The envoys answer humbly, ‘We are your servants’, and tell their story. They have come, they say, ‘because of the fame of the LORD your God’ (verse 9). They have heard what he did in Egypt and to the two kings east of the Jordan. Then they show the evidence. The bread was warm when they left home. The wineskins were new.

“Then the men of Israel sampled their provisions, but did not seek the counsel of the LORD. And Joshua made a treaty of peace with them to let them live, and the leaders of the congregation swore an oath to them” (verses 14-15).
passages.hearers:
Gibeon was not a village. It was an important town in the hills a few miles northwest of Jerusalem, at the head of a small league of four towns. It lay directly in Israel's path.

The disguise is aimed at one particular law. Deuteronomy told Israel that it could offer terms of peace to cities far away, but that it was to make no treaty with the peoples of Canaan itself. The Gibeonites seem to know this. So they do not pretend to be strong or rich. They pretend to be from far off, because that is the one thing that could save them.

What they say about God is true, and it is much like what Rahab said. They have heard of the LORD, and they believe the reports. Like her, they decide that it is hopeless to fight him. Unlike her, they come with a lie about themselves. The Hebrew word for the way they act can mean craftiness in a bad sense or shrewdness in a good one. The story leaves the reader to weigh both.

‘We are your servants’ was the language a weaker party used when it asked a stronger king for protection.

Israel's mistake is told in one line. The men looked at the bread. They tested the evidence with their own eyes and hands, and it was convincing. What they did not do was ask God. Joshua had been told that he could seek God's direction through the priest. No one did. This is the second time in three chapters that Israel has acted on what seemed obvious without asking, and the first was the defeat at Ai.

A treaty in the ancient world was a sacred thing, sworn in the name of a god who would hold the swearers to it. Once the leaders swore, the matter was no longer only between Israel and Gibeon.
passages.later:
The law they were working around is in Deuteronomy: “When you approach a city to fight against it, you are to make an offer of peace” (Deuteronomy 20:10), a rule the next verses limit to ‘all the cities that are far away from you’ (Deuteronomy 20:15).

Joshua had been told how to ask for God's direction: “He shall stand before Eleazar the priest, who will seek counsel for him before the LORD” (Numbers 27:21).

A proverb warns about the kind of confidence the men of Israel showed: “Trust in the LORD with all your heart, and lean not on your own understanding” (Proverbs 3:5).
passages.asks: The men of Israel checked the bread and did not ask God. Ask what decision you are making on evidence that seems plain enough not to need prayer. Then think about the Gibeonites. They believed what they had heard about God and came the only way they could think of. Ask whether you have ever come to God with half the truth about yourself, and what it would be to come with all of it.

passages.happening:
Three days later Israel learns the truth. The Gibeonites are neighbors. Israel marches to their towns: Gibeon, Chephirah, Beeroth and Kiriath-jearim (verse 17).

“But the Israelites did not attack them, because the leaders of the congregation had sworn an oath to them by the LORD, the God of Israel. And the whole congregation grumbled against the leaders” (verse 18).

The leaders hold firm. “We have sworn an oath to them by the LORD, the God of Israel, and now we cannot touch them” (verse 19). The Gibeonites will live. They will be woodcutters and water carriers for the whole community (verse 21).

Joshua calls the Gibeonites in and asks why they lied. They answer honestly at last. They had been told that the LORD commanded Moses to give Israel all the land. “So we greatly feared for our lives because of you, and that is why we have done this. Now we are in your hands. Do to us whatever seems good and right to you” (verses 24-25).

Joshua protects them from the people, ‘and they did not kill the Gibeonites’ (verse 26). He makes them woodcutters and water carriers ‘for the congregation of the LORD and for the altar’ (verse 27).
passages.hearers:
The people grumble, and a reader can see why. They have been tricked. The law seemed to be on their side. Their leaders had been careless.

The leaders do not defend their mistake. They also do not use the trick as a way out. The oath was sworn ‘by the LORD, the God of Israel’. To break it would be to treat God's name as something that could be put aside when it became costly. So they keep a promise they should never have made, to people who lied to get it.

Joshua says the Gibeonites are ‘under a curse’ and gives them hard work. Cutting wood and carrying water were among the heaviest daily tasks. The hard question below looks at whether that was just.

But look at where the work is done. It is ‘for the altar’. The sacrifices needed great amounts of wood and water. A people who had been under sentence of death end up serving at the center of Israel's worship. They are spared, they are protected by Israel's leader from Israel's own people, and they are bound to the house of God.

The book has now shown two groups of Canaanites who lived. Rahab came with faith and kindness. The Gibeonites came with fear and a lie. Both said that they had heard what the LORD had done, and both were let in. The kings in verse 1 heard the same reports and chose war.
passages.later:
The oath was still in force generations later. King Saul tried to wipe out the Gibeonites, and in David's time a famine was traced to it: “It is because of the blood shed by Saul and his family, because he killed the Gibeonites” (2 Samuel 21:1).

A psalm asks who may live in God's presence, and one answer is the person ‘who does not revise a costly oath’ (Psalm 15:4).

After the exile, when the wall of Jerusalem was rebuilt, their descendants were there with the builders: ‘Melatiah the Gibeonite’ and ‘the men of Gibeon’ (Nehemiah 3:7).
passages.hard:
Why did an oath won by a lie still bind Israel? And was the sentence on the Gibeonites just?

Modern law would treat an agreement gained by fraud as void, and a reader may wonder why Israel did not. The text gives its own answer. The oath was sworn in the LORD's name, and to break it would dishonor that name and bring his anger (verse 20). Later Scripture agrees. When Saul broke the treaty, the land suffered (2 Samuel 21:1-2).

Readers weigh the leaders' mistake in two ways. Some stress that God used it to spare people who had turned toward him. Others stress that the mistake was real, and that it left inside Israel a group the law had told Israel not to make terms with. The text supports both, and these notes do not choose.

The forced service is troubling too. Readers have noted three things. It took the place of a death sentence and was not added to one. The Gibeonites accepted it (verse 25). And service at the sanctuary brought them near to Israel's worship. Others simply say that the arrangement belongs to the hard world of its time, which the Bible reports without approving every part of it.

Nothing here makes forced labor right, and nothing here gives anyone today a reason to hold another person in service against their will.

A word for anyone who is being held, owned or forced to work today. It is not your fault. You are not the property of the people who hold you. If you can, please tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Israel's leaders kept a promise that had been tricked out of them, because they had made it in God's name. Ask what promise you have made that has become costly, and whether you are looking for a way out of it. Then think about the Gibeonites. They came by a lie and were kept by an oath. Ask whether you believe God holds on to people who came to him for poor reasons, and whether you count yourself among them.
